summary: Describes SDXF, an all-purpose format for exchanging structured data as a file format or over a network. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a way to pack information into labeled boxes inside boxes so any computer can unpack it the same way.

questions: how do i read sdxf data
subtitle: A portable, self-describing format for exchanging structured data.

tldr.problem: Applications need a way to exchange structured data across different computers, languages, and architectures without losing information or compatibility.
tldr.mechanism: SDXF organizes data as nested chunks—labeled containers that hold typed data (text, numbers, binary)—and specifies how to encode them in a platform-independent binary format using big-endian byte order and standardized character encodings.
tldr.outcome: The format is self-describing: any program can read SDXF data without knowing in advance what it contains. It supports compression, encryption, arrays, and platform-independent data representation, though XML and ASN.1 became more widely adopted for similar purposes.

facts.label: Data types
facts.value: 7 (structure, bit string, numeric, character, float, UTF-8, pending)

today: RFC 3072 is informational and has not been obsoleted. SDXF was designed as a general-purpose exchange format but was never widely adopted in the Internet community. Today, XML, JSON, and Protocol Buffers serve similar roles with broader industry support.

sections.title: What SDXF Does
sections.content:
The Structured Data eXchange Format (SDXF) is an all-purpose format for storing and transmitting structured data. Its purpose is to allow arbitrary combinations of numbers, text, and binary data to flow between different kinds of computers—those with different processors, memory architectures, or character encodings—while remaining readable on both ends.

SDXF is self-describing: every SDXF file tells a reader what it contains without requiring external documentation or prior knowledge. The format also supports compression and encryption, making it suitable for files, network communication, remote procedure calls, documents, and business data exchange.
sections.eli5: SDXF is like a universal shipping container format. No matter what computer receives an SDXF package, it knows how to open and understand it.

sections.title: Chunks: The Building Block
sections.content:
All data in SDXF is organized as chunks. A chunk consists of a small header (6 bytes) and a content body. The header contains a chunk ID (a number from 1 to 65,535), a flags byte that describes the data type, and a 3-byte length field telling how many bytes follow.

Chunks can be elementary (they hold raw data like a string or number) or structured (they contain a list of other chunks, building a hierarchy). This nesting allows SDXF to represent any hierarchical data structure. A structured chunk can hold dozens of child chunks, each of which can itself be structured.
sections.eli5: A chunk is a labeled box. Some boxes hold stuff directly; others hold more labeled boxes inside.

sections.title: Data Types and Encoding
sections.content:
The flags byte in each chunk header specifies the data type. SDXF defines seven basic types: pending structures (incomplete chunks), structures, bit strings, numeric values, character text, floating-point numbers, and UTF-8 text. The flags also control whether the chunk is compressed, encrypted, or is an array.

To ensure platform independence, SDXF normalizes binary representation: all numbers are stored in big-endian order (most significant byte first), matching IP network byte order. Character data defaults to ISO 8859-1 (Latin 1) encoding, though UTF-8 is explicitly supported. A short chunk optimizes small data: instead of using a separate content area, it stores up to 3 bytes of data directly in the length field.
sections.eli5: Each box is labeled with what kind of stuff is inside—a number, text, or more boxes. Everything is stored the same way on every computer so nothing gets scrambled.

sections.title: Writing and Reading
sections.content:
SDXF provides an API (a set of functions) for building and reading chunks. To write data, a program calls init to start, then repeatedly calls create to add chunks and leave to close a structured chunk. To read data, a program calls init, then enter to open a structured chunk, next to move to the next chunk, extract to read the content of an elementary chunk, and leave to exit a structure.

The API handles all the binary encoding and decoding work; programmers do not manually manipulate bits. When compression or encryption is enabled, the API handles that transparently—the programmer just tells the functions which chunks to compress, and they do it automatically.
sections.eli5: You do not have to think about numbers and bytes. You just call functions like create and extract, and they take care of packing and unpacking.

sections.title: Compression, Encryption, and Comparisons
sections.content:
SDXF supports optional compression (to reduce size) and encryption (to protect confidentiality) on individual chunks or entire structures. A flag bit marks which chunks are compressed or encrypted; the API handles the mechanics.

The RFC acknowledges that SDXF competes with two established formats: ASN.1, which is standardized for structured data but complex; and XML, which is human-readable and widely supported but verbose. SDXF is compact and self-describing but never gained the industry adoption of either. For most purposes today, XML or JSON would be preferred.
sections.eli5: SDXF can lock a box with a password or squeeze it smaller. Other formats like XML do similar things, but they became more popular.
